name: advanced-planning
description: Create visual plans with a clear implementation path and reviewable details.
body:
---
name: advanced-planning
---
<!-- mc-skill v6 -->

# Advanced Planning

Build a plan that answers, visually and in under 30 seconds: **what changes, where, how it flows, and how we know it works**.

## Deliverables

2. Start from `assets/plan-template.html`; adapt its components instead of creating another visual system.
3. Present a compact text equivalent in the final response so approval never depends on the canvas.
5. `plan.html` plus the chat response are the entire deliverable. Do not also write the plan, a summary, or any equivalent to a separate `.md`/`.txt` file anywhere in the canvas directory or the project — one canvas file, one chat reply, nothing else on disk.

## Investigate before drawing

Ground every visual in repository evidence: concrete files, symbols, boundaries, data flow, dependencies, states, tests, and rollout implications. Do not narrate exploration or repeat the request.

## Visual-first content order

Keep this hierarchy. Remove a visual only when it genuinely does not apply.

1. **Outcome** — a concrete one-sentence page title plus one short supporting line.
2. **Impact strip** — 3-5 compact facts such as files changed, files added, flows affected, migrations, and risk. Use numbers or short labels, never prose cards.
3. **Important** — at most three decisions or risks. Use “No blockers” when empty.
4. **Experience preview** — for UI or interaction work, show a labeled before/after wireframe or state sequence. For non-UI work, replace it with an input/output, request/response, schema, or lifecycle visual. Never show a decorative mockup.
5. **Change inventory** — compact tables for **Added**, **Changed**, and **Removed**. Every row names a path or symbol, the exact change, and its purpose. Use “None” rows rather than omitting groups.
6. **System map** — one small architecture/data-flow diagram with 3-7 nodes. Include its Mermaid source in an HTML comment and render an equivalent diagram with HTML/CSS so the file stays self-contained.
7. **User workflow** — one small happy-path or state-flow diagram. Branch only for meaningful failure or alternate states.
8. **Implementation lanes** — a compact table of ordered phases, ownership boundaries, dependencies, and completion signals. Keep detail in cells to one sentence.
9. **Verification matrix** — a table mapping behavior/risk to the exact automated or manual check and expected result.

## Visual density rules

- Target **70% visual structure / 30% prose**. Prefer tables, labeled diagrams, timelines, state grids, diffs, and wireframes over paragraphs.
- Keep prose blocks to two sentences and list items to one line. If text becomes long, convert it to a table or diagram.
- Show UI work at recognizable fidelity: navigation, controls, labels, states, and changed regions. Use annotations to identify behavior; do not polish irrelevant decoration.
- Use before/after comparisons for changed experiences and state sequences for new interactions.
- Use compact tables for file changes, API/schema deltas, state transitions, permissions, and test coverage.
- Diagrams must encode relationships. Avoid a diagram that simply repeats a list.
- The canvas should remain understandable at a glance without reading every cell.

## Visual contract

- Palette: `#121212` page, `#181818` surface, `#242424` rules, `#ffffff` primary, `#5ac8fa` accent, `#f5b451` warning, `#ff6b6b` danger, `#4fd98b` success.
- Use 12-14px body copy, a constrained reading width, compact spacing, and strong labels.
- Prefer flat sections and rules. No nested-card wall, gradients, glass effects, oversized headings, or pill overload.
- Reserve white emphasis for the main outcome. Red means genuine breakage, deletion, or required attention.
- Bold only decision-bearing phrases. Use monospace for paths, symbols, commands, routes, and data shapes.
- Use inline SVG or simple CSS shapes when they clarify a flow. Do not use remote assets or decorative emoji.
- Keep HTML self-contained, responsive, keyboard/text-selection friendly, and printable.

## Final response format

Write this directly as your final chat message — never as a file. Use the same information hierarchy in a compact Markdown form:

- one-sentence outcome;
- important decisions or blockers;
- Added / Changed / Removed tables;
- ordered implementation lanes;
- verification matrix.

Do not duplicate every visual annotation in prose. Link to `plan.html` when available.

## Quality check

Before publishing, confirm:

- a reader can name the outcome and affected flow in 10 seconds;
- UI changes have a before/after or state mockup;
- added, changed, and removed items are explicit;
- diagrams match the actual code boundaries;
- prose is shorter than the visual structures it explains;
- every verification row has an observable expected result;
- all placeholder guidance and unused template content is removed.

name: ui-mockup
description: Before implementing a UI, generate exactly three distinct visual directions as self-contained HTML files so the user can flip between them and pick a favorite.

name: ui-mockup
description: Before implementing a UI, generate exactly three distinct visual directions as self-contained HTML files so the user can flip between them and pick a favorite.
---
<!-- mc-skill v2 -->

# UI Mockup

When asked to design or build a UI and this skill is attached, do NOT go straight to implementation. First produce exactly three alternative visual directions for the same content so the user can compare and choose.

## Output location (critical)


## Rules

1. Same content and information architecture in all three; what changes is the visual philosophy: layout, typography, color, density, and mood. Make the three genuinely different (for example: minimal-airy vs dense-professional vs bold-expressive), not three tints of one design.
2. Each file is fully self-contained: inline CSS/JS only, no external network resources, system font stacks.
3. Start each file with an HTML comment naming and describing its direction in one line, e.g. `<!-- Variant 2: "Terminal" - dense, monospaced, high-contrast dark -->`.
4. Polish matters: these are pitches, so spacing, hierarchy, and alignment must be tight in all three.
5. After saving, list the three paths with a one-line description of each direction, then stop and wait for the user to pick one before implementing anything.

name: skeleton
description: When concepting a website, app, page, or UI feature, generate a single self-contained HTML skeleton of the concept and save it for visual preview before any real implementation begins.

---
name: skeleton
description: When concepting a website, app, page, or UI feature, generate a single self-contained HTML skeleton of the concept and save it for visual preview before any real implementation begins.
---
<!-- mc-skill v2 -->

# Skeleton


## Output location (critical)


## Rules

1. One single self-contained file: all CSS and JS inline. No external network resources (no CDN scripts, no web fonts, no remote images). Use system font stacks and CSS shapes/gradients as placeholders.
2. Semantic structure: real header/nav/main/section/footer landmarks matching the described concept, with realistic placeholder copy (not lorem ipsum walls; short plausible labels and headings).
3. Dark-friendly, neutral default styling: clean spacing, restrained grayscale palette with one accent. The goal is structure and hierarchy, not final art.
4. Keep it fast to scan: this is a wireframe with taste, not a finished design.
5. After saving, tell the user the exact path you wrote and a one-line summary of the layout choices, then stop for feedback. Do not continue building the real product until the user reacts.
